description: Equipo de ing. de software avanzada, automatización e IA. Construiremos una plataforma interactiva de alto rendimiento para procesar y visualizar grandes volúmenes de datos de la Tierra de la NASA, detectando tendencias climáticas con rigor analítico.
summary:
When a wildfire spreads, decisions made in the first hours determine whether it stays a forest fire or becomes a catastrophe. In January 2026, wildfires in Chile's Biobío region killed 21 people and destroyed more than 2,000 homes. One of our team members saw the damage in Tomé days later.

SARWatch is an interactive territorial analysis platform built to support those decisions. It shows where heat is detected hour by hour (GOES) and where the wind is pushing it (ERA5), so users can see which areas lie in the fire's path. It then uses Sentinel-2 and NISAR L-band radar to show what the fire left behind and how the land evolves over the following months, with a time series for any point on the map.

It addresses the challenge by turning NISAR radar into evidence anyone can explore, and by stating clearly what the data can and cannot prove. It matters because every hour gained can protect lives, homes, and the native flora and fauna that disappear with the forest. SARWatch is a first step toward an operational tool for emergency teams.
details:
SARWatch is a web-based territorial analysis platform that brings satellite evidence of wildfires and surface change in Chile into a single, readable view. Users select an area, compare observations across dates, check weather conditions and export the evidence for review. The platform integrates thermal detections from NASA FIRMS and NOAA GOES, weather data from Open-Meteo, Sentinel-2 optical imagery, NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar, elevation data and official delineations from Copernicus.

Its main case study covers Concepción, Penco and Tomé, in the Biobío region, where it combines records of the January 2026 wildfire with official delineations and NISAR observations acquired afterwards, in February, June and October. A second case presents Sentinel-2 imagery from before and after the February 2024 Viña del Mar wildfire, kept clearly separate from the 2026 radar observations.

Satellite evidence of this kind usually demands specialized software and training. By placing maps, acquisition dates and sources side by side, SARWatch makes that evidence accessible, traceable and reproducible. Our aim is to help communities, researchers and emergency specialists understand how a wildfire affects people, homes and native flora and fauna, and to provide a foundation for future work with emergency teams.

The interface is built with JavaScript, React and MapLibre GL, and the backend with Python and FastAPI. Scientific and geospatial libraries read the NISAR products, prepare the imagery, transform coordinates and evaluate models. The application runs on Google Cloud Run, with derived products stored in Cloud Storage, and the code is public on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license. AI coding assistants supported programming, review and documentation, as declared within the application.

What sets the project apart is that it joins several time scales in one visual experience: thermal detections within hours, weather conditions, optical burn signals within days, and the evolution of the terrain through radar over months. It also includes an exploratory model that ranks cells by surveillance priority over a 12-day horizon, and it reports the evaluation openly: an AUC of 0.632 on held-out dates, with 44 positive cases.

Throughout development we weighed the clarity of the interface, the dates and resolution of each sensor, uncertainty, data provenance and operating cost. We chose to state the limits plainly. NISAR is not presented as a thermal sensor or a live observation, the model requires further validation, and the platform does not calculate fire trajectories, spread rates or safe routes for brigades.
